analysis.one_liner: Counts GI Bill and military education benefits as federal money for-profit colleges may receive.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in December 2017, sent to two subcommittees, and died in committee at the end of the 115th Congress without ever getting a hearing or a vote; it had a sponsor and two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires for-profit colleges to get at least 10% of their revenue from non-federal sources, or lose access to federal student aid. Today, GI Bill benefits and military tuition assistance count toward that 10% — meaning a college can be funded almost entirely by taxpayers and still pass the test. This bill would count those military and veteran benefits as federal money, and would cut off all federal education aid — including Pentagon and Veterans Affairs programs — to any for-profit college that fails the test for two years in a row.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members, veterans, and their families, whose education benefits would no longer be treated as an unlimited subsidy that for-profit colleges can count on. Taxpayers benefit because federal education dollars would face an actual limit, and students would be steered toward schools that don't depend on the federal government for nearly all their revenue.

how_it_helps.text: For-profit colleges would have to count GI Bill benefits (title 38 programs) and Pentagon education programs (title 10) as federal revenue, ending the loophole that lets schools pass the 10% test while being funded nearly entirely by taxpayers.

If a for-profit college fails the requirement two years in a row, it would be barred from at least two years of all federal educational assistance — student aid, Defense Department programs, and Veterans Affairs programs — and would need two consecutive years of compliance to get back in.

The Education Secretary would notify the Defense and Veterans Affairs Secretaries, who must cut off their own education programs to ineligible schools and publicly post the school's name, how it failed the requirement, and how long it will be ineligible.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges that rely heavily on military and veteran education benefits would lose that dependable revenue stream, and some would fail the revised test and lose access to federal education programs. Students enrolled at such a school when it lost eligibility would need to finish their education elsewhere.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges dependent on GI Bill revenue

drawbacks.text: Students enrolled at a school that loses eligibility would lose access to federal education funding at that institution, and the bill bars that school from all federal education programs for at least two years, forcing mid-program transfers.

The bill creates a cross-agency enforcement system — Education, Defense, Veterans Affairs, Homeland Security, and the military departments each must enforce a shared ineligibility determination — which adds administrative coordination that could be slow or uneven in practice.

A school failing the test by a narrow margin faces the same minimum two-year penalty as a badly out-of-compliance one, because the bill sets a floor of 'not less than two' fiscal years of ineligibility with no proportionality.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — ending a loophole that lets for-profit colleges treat soldiers' and veterans' benefits as if they weren't federal money — is aimed at a real, well-documented pattern of those institutions recruiting service members. Its main cost falls on students at schools that lose eligibility, who would have to move, though the public posting requirement would give prospective students warning. The penalty structure is blunt. On balance it is a targeted consumer protection for a specific population rather than a universal benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three committees and two subcommittees in December 2017 and January 2018, none of which ever acted on it, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Speier introduced the bill on December 12, 2017, joined by Rep. Walter Jones (R) and Rep. Mark Takano (D).
It was referred to the Education and the Workforce, Armed Services, and Veterans' Affairs Committees, and then to the Economic Opportunity and Military Personnel subcommittees.
No committee or subcommittee held a markup, hearing on the bill, or floor action, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges kept the ability to count GI Bill and military tuition assistance as non-federal revenue, so nothing changed for them; service members and veterans remained exposed to schools funded almost entirely by federal education benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to count military and veteran education benefits as federal revenue for the 90/10 rule.

for.name: Rep. Walter Jones
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House committee leadership (Education and the Workforce; Armed Services; Veterans' Affairs)
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill but never scheduled a markup, hearing on the bill, or floor consideration during the remaining year of the Congress.

against.name: For-profit higher education industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending the 90/10 rule to military and veteran education funding, which would have exposed schools heavily dependent on GI Bill revenue to losing federal aid eligibility.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; sponsorship was small and bipartisan — one Democratic sponsor, with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor — so the parties' positions were never tested.

industries.note: These schools would have to count GI Bill and military tuition assistance as federal revenue, and schools failing the test two years running would lose access to all federal education programs for at least two years. Many for-profit colleges recruit service members and veterans because those benefits flow directly to the school, so the bill threatens a core revenue base.

Schools that do not rely on federal money for nearly all their revenue would face no change, while competitors losing eligibility would push enrollments toward compliant schools. Students would be safer choosing them.
